title: WhatsApp and Facebook (end-of-term exam, November 2020)
text: Summary of the six pre-reading articles (Forbes 2014, Fast Company 2018 and 2020, Wall Street Journal 2018, Inc. 2019, Fortune 2019).

WhatsApp. Jan Koum grew up in a village near Kiev, in a home where his parents avoided the phone for fear of state surveillance, and emigrated to California at 16. At Yahoo he befriended Brian Acton; both were rejected by Facebook. In 2009 Koum founded WhatsApp; when he wanted to give up, Acton convinced him to continue and brought in seed money from ex-Yahoo friends. The founders worked from cafés and an unmarked back door in a shared warehouse; they refused publicity (“marketing and press kick up dust”), resisted venture capital for a long time and accepted Sequoia only after it promised not to push advertising. There was no company sign: “we all know where we work”.

WhatsApp's culture is built on focus: a simple, efficient product without ads, no growth hacking, growth only by word of mouth, very small engineering teams with few meetings, quiet offices (“Focus is the new F-word” magnets, “please keep noise to a minimum” signs) and strong convictions about privacy – end-to-end encryption completed in 2016. With fewer than 250 employees in 2018 it served more than a billion users, partly by using Facebook's recruiting machine and infrastructure.

The acquisition. Facebook bought WhatsApp in 2014 for $19 billion. Mark Zuckerberg promised autonomy and agreed that ads were not the right model for messaging. Facebook's own model is a huge advertising business based on user data, and its culture favours trying many things and fast growth. From around 2016, Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg pushed to integrate WhatsApp and monetise it: targeted ads (e.g. in the Status feature), more features, more “business flexibility” on encryption. The WhatsApp team moved to Facebook's Menlo Park campus – a bustling place with restaurants and ice-cream shops modelled on Disneyland – but stayed apart; its quiet signs were mocked (“Welcome to WhatsApp – shut up!”), and its larger desks, better bathrooms and private meeting rooms irritated staff in a company that prides itself on egalitarianism. The founders' alternative revenue ideas were dismissed (“that doesn't scale”).

The split. Acton, described as the team's “moral compass”, resigned in September 2017 as plans for ads advanced, leaving large unvested stock behind, and later tweeted “It is time. #deletefacebook”. Koum, who sat on Facebook's board, stayed eight more months and left in April 2018 without confronting Zuckerberg. Instagram's founders, who had enjoyed similar autonomy and felt starved of resources, left later in 2018. By 2020 Facebook was integrating its apps.

Facebook's culture. Long ranked the best place to work in Silicon Valley, Facebook was described by former employees in 2019 as cult-like: pressure to appear happy and enthusiastic internally and on social media; criticism for missing after-hours team events; peer reviews by five self-chosen colleagues that make alliances a survival skill and discourage dissent; stack ranking twice a year into seven categories, with about 15 % placed in the lowest ones (risk of being fired, careers blocked); leavers labelled “regrettable” or “non-regrettable”, which can affect their future in the industry. Facebook's spokesperson rejected the claims as unrepresentative.

Incentives. In 2019, after the Cambridge Analytica scandal and other crises, Facebook changed its bonus formula: instead of six factors such as user growth, sharing and product quality, bonuses for its ~36,000 employees would depend on progress on social issues (misinformation, hate speech, safety, privacy), new experiences, support for businesses and better communication. Management admitted there was no easy formula to measure progress on these goals.
